docs.title: DESIGN DOCUMENTATION
docs.text:
Welcome to Bear Metal's Design Docs! From here, you can learn various different aspects of our design process as well as other related content!

For any suggestions/feedback, feel free to DM @Matthaeusssss via Discord 🤓

  • COTS Library

    Learn about what stocks, and Commercial-Off-The-Shelf products we use in our designs

  • CAD Fundamentals

    Every designers foundation to their mansion of knowledge, CAD is the favorite pass-time of every designer... right?...

  • Iteration Process

    Continuing to iterate through the season is our key to success... here's how we do it effectively ^

  • Inter-Subteam Knowledge

    Isolated designers are what lead us to making poorly integrated robots, let's not do that!

  • Mechanism Challenges

    Currated challenges to help develop a breadth of design knowledge in making beautiful designs (yippee!) ^

  • Organization/Documents

    With the sheer size of our team, we need to maximize our ability to communicate with eachother, here's how ^

  • Physics-In-Design

    For all the nerds out there and those who are groaning right now... Yes, math is involved in designing robots.

  • Strategic Design

    "How do we determine what to build during the build-season?"

    • here's our thought process!

  • Sustainability

    Very wise words from the yee olden design leads... and other words of advise to creating a sustainable design program!

  • External Resources

    There are plenty of tools and resources out there for designers, here are some of them ^

📝 Note

This functions as a culmination of both the returning/new membership training materials as well as effective pass-down of knowledge of various aspects regarding the design of our robots.

docs.title: Electronics Documentation
docs.text:
This site is a knowledge base for the electrical components and practices we use on the electrical subteam. Expect missing information as I am actively working on compiling information. If you have any questions or would like to suggest a change, let me know by DMing me on Discord! (@pra1ries)

~ Corbin

  • Motors

    Here you can find information about motors and motor related hardware.

  • Electrical Components

    Here you can find information about different electrical components.

  • Pneumatic Components

    Here you can find information about pneumatic components.

  • Concepts

    Here you can find information about concepts we use in electronics.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: These are some concepts you will be expected to know, as they are a fundamental part of understanding how an electrical system functions.

docs.title: Ohm's Law
docs.text:
Ohm's Law, put simply, is the equation V = IR, where V is voltage, I is amperage, and R is resistance.

In order to understand Ohm's Law, you need to understand what voltage, amperage, and resistance are.

docs.title: Voltage
docs.text: Voltage is the measure of potential difference in the charge of the positive and negative terminals of a system. This is measured in Volts (V).

docs.title: Amperage
docs.text: Amperage is the magnitude of the charge being transferred. This is measured in Amps or Amperes (A).

docs.title: Resistance
docs.text: Resistance is the measure of opposition to the flow of an electrical current. This is measured in Ohms (Ω).

docs.title: Circuits
docs.text: Depending on how circuits are wired, the amperage, voltage, and resistance can change at certain points. In this section we will explore the concepts of parallel and series circuits.

docs.title: Parallel Circuits
docs.text:
If you have two batteries wired into a circuit in parallel, the total amperage of the circuit will be the sum of the amperage of the batteries.

In this theoretical parallel circuit, the positive terminals of both batteries will be connected to the same wire, this wire will serve as the positive wire for the circuit. The same goes for the negative wire, it will be connected to the negative terminal of both batteries.

docs.title: Series Circuits
docs.text:
If you have two batteries wired into a circuit in series, the total voltage of the circuit will be the sum of the voltage of the batteries.

In this theoretical circuit, the negative terminal of battery 1 serves as the negative terminal for the whole circuit. The positive terminal of battery 1 is connected to the negative terminal of battery 2. The positive terminal of battery 2 serves as the positive terminal for the whole circuit.

docs.title: Electrical System Components
docs.text: Below are several electrical system components that you may be working with on our robots.

docs.title: PDH
docs.text: The PDH distributes power from the battery throughout the robot's electrical system. We typically use the PDH due to it's ports being easier to open, it having a native voltage display, and other features not available on the PDP.

docs.title: PDP
docs.text: The PDP serves the same purpose as the PDH. We don't typically use the PDP on competition robots due to the fact that it lacks features available on the PDH.

docs.title: VRM
docs.text: The VRM is used to regulate voltage, specifically to components that require less power and use smaller gauge wire.

docs.title: Five-Star
docs.text: The Five-Star allows CAN to be routed to other components individually rather than in a daisy chain.

docs.title: Radio
docs.text: The Radio allows the robot to be controlled wirelessly through the driver's station. Below is an image of the new radio that will become standard for the 2025 season.

docs.title: RPM
docs.text: The RPM is used to easily splice power into an ethernet cable, which will be used to power the radio using PoE.

docs.title: CANCoder
docs.text: CANCoders are used to find how much rotating mechanisms have rotated and relay that data through the CAN system. The CANCoder itself is a small PCB, but is placed in close proximity to a cylindrical magnet that rotates with the rotating mechanism (for example, in an axle) whilst the CANCoder remains static. The CANCoder uses the magnet to find rotational data.

docs.title: Main Breaker
docs.text: The Main Breaker interrupts the positive wire from the battery before it goes to the PDH or PDP. The large red button will disconnect power, and pushing the lever back in will restore power. When connecting the main breaker, make sure the "aux" terminal is connected to the PDP or PDH.

docs.title: RoboRIO
docs.text: The RoboRIO is the code that runs robot code. It is an extremely important part of the robot (and expensive), so please try not to break it.

docs.title: Pigeon 2.0
docs.text: The Pigeon 2.0 IMU is a gyroscope that assists the robot in knowing where it is on the field. Typically this component will be placed somewhere near the center of the robot.

docs.title: RSL
docs.text: The RSL is a large orange light that displays the status of the robot. Solid means that the robot is powered on, but not enabled. Blinking means the robot is powered on and enabled. If the light is not on, the robot either doesn't have power or the RSL is not connected correctly.

docs.title: CANivore
docs.text: The CANivore is a CAN-to-USB adapter that allows us to create an entirely new CAN network. This allows us to split all CAN connected components in our robot into different groups. For example, in the 2024 season we had all of our mechanisms daisy chained to the RoboRIO's CAN port, and we had our swerve motors and CANCoders daisy chained to a CANivore. One of the downsides to CANivores is that we need to manually add terminating resistors to the end of daisy chained systems that use a CANivore.

docs.title: Motors
docs.text: Motors are a crucial part of nearly every moving mechanism. Below are several motors and motor related hardware that we use.

docs.title: Kraken X60
docs.text: On our competition robots we mainly use Kraken X60 brushless motors. These motors have a lot of power behind them and have a built in motor controller, unlike the NEO series of motors which require external motor controllers. Krakens typically use 10AWG wire for power.

docs.title: NEO Series
docs.text:
WARNING:

These motors use JST crimps, which we do not like because they are a pain to fix when the wires break. The JST wires coming from the NEO motors are 24AWG, so they are very fragile. DO NOT bend JST WIRES at sharp angles, especially near the crimp, because they WILL break.

Note:

It is unlikely for us to use these components on competition robots due to us transitioning to using Krakens, but they might be used during prototyping.

NEO v1.1 and NEO 550 brushless motors require a Spark MAX motor controller in order for them to be controlled. Be careful when running NEO 550s, they are outrunner motors, which means that the shell of the motor rotates along with the shaft. The most obvious difference between NEO v1.1 motors and NEO 550s is that NEO v1.1 motors are significantly larger and have much more torque. NEO 550 and NEO v1.1 motors also use different size wires for power. NEO 550s use 16AWG wire for power, and NEO v1.1 motors use 12AWG wire for power.

docs.title: Spark MAX
docs.text:
Note:

It is unlikely for us to use this component on competition robots due to us transitioning to using Krakens, but it might be used during prototyping.

The Spark MAX is a motor controller that we use for both NEO v1.1 motors and NEO 550s.

docs.title: Pneumatic System Components
docs.text:
Note:

Unlike electrical components, we will not use pneumatics every year. The decision of whether or not we use pneumatics ultimately comes down to how we decide to approach the year's game.

Below are several pneumatic system components that you may be working with on our robots.

docs.title: Compressor
docs.text: The compressor is the starting point for every pneumatics system. It compresses air into the accumulators for use in the pneumatic system.

docs.title: Accumulator
docs.text: The accumulator(s) store compressed air for future use in the pneumatic system. They hold up to 125 PSI, however we regulate stored pressure to about 120 to be safe. Pressure coming out of the accumulator to the rest of the system should be regulated to 60 PSI.

docs.title: Regulator
docs.text: Pressure regulators regulate how much pressure is allowed in a certain part of the pneumatics system. We typically have one regulator before the accumulator set to 120 PSI (stored pressure), and one after the accumulator set to 60 PSI (working pressure).

docs.title: Pressure Gauge
docs.text: The pressure gauge displays the PSI of the section it is placed in the pneumatic system. We typically put these right after regulators.

docs.title: Manifold
docs.text: The manifold distributes compressed air to pneumatic components such as cylinders. The actuation of these pneumatic components are controlled by pneumatic solenoids.

docs.title: Solenoids
docs.text: Pneumatic solenoids allow us to control the actuation of our pneumatics remotely. However, you can actuate pneumatics by pressing the small blue buttons on the solenoids if you are testing a mechanism.

docs.title: Pressure Relief Valve
docs.text: The pressure relief valve is a mechanical version of the pressure switch. The pressure relief valve is calibrated to 125 PSI (which is the maximum rated pressure of the accumulators). When the pressure exceeds that, the pressure relief valve pops open briefly to release pressure. From first-hand experience, this is VERY loud. Do not intentionally activate the pressure relief valve when you are near it.

docs.title: Pressure Switch
docs.text: The pressure switch is a digital version of the relief valve that functions slightly differently. Instead of releasing pressure, it stops the compressor when it reaches a certain pressure (the ones we use do this at 115 PSI).

docs.title: Cylinders
docs.text: Pneumatic Cylinders use pneumatic pressure in order to actuate in a linear motion.

docs.title: Dump Valve
docs.text: The dump valve is typically a valve we have connected at the beginning of the system that, when activated, will relieve pressure stored in the system. We use this after we are done testing/using pneumatics or after we complete a match (if there are pneumatics on the robot).

docs.title: Programming Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to Bear Metal's Programming Docs! From here, you can learn the noble art of robot control, one line of code at a time.

For any suggestions/feedback, feel free to DM @RENIE JOSHI via Teams 🤓

  • Java Fundamentals

    The concepts and syntax of everything we write. Here's your crash course in the language of our robot code.

  • Robot Libraries

    WPILib, vendor libraries, and everything in between that make the robot actually do things.

  • Command-Based Architecture

    Commands, mechanisms, and how we keep our code from morphing into one 2000-line Robot.java. Learn how we organize code and why we do it this way.

  • Control Theory

    PID loops, tuning, and the math behind making the robot go where you want. For those who enjoy math that actually matters.

  • Simulation & Testing

    Because breaking the real robot is expensive.

  • Sustainability

    Very wise words from the yee olden programming leads... and other words of advice on writing code for future members.

  • External Resources

    Tools and resources from the wider FRC community.
